patches.old: Despite central tolerance, some self-reactive lymphocytes escape into the periphery—estimates suggest roughly 20–30% of mature naïve T cells carry receptors with some self-reactivity.
patches.new: Despite central tolerance, some self-reactive lymphocytes inevitably escape into the periphery.
patches.reason: The specific 20–30% figure is not an established value; removed it.

patches.old:
**Late-phase response (4–8 hours)**:
- Synthesis and release of **leukotrienes** (LTC4, LTD4—potent bronchoconstrictors, ~1000× more potent than histamine) and **prostaglandins** (PGD2)
- Cytokine production (IL-4, IL-5, TNF-α) that recruits and activates eosinophils, causing tissue inflammation
patches.new:
- Within minutes, activated mast cells also synthesize lipid mediators from arachidonic acid: **leukotrienes** (LTC4, LTD4—potent, sustained bronchoconstrictors, far more potent than histamine) and **prostaglandin D2**

**Late-phase response (hours later, typically ~4–12 hours)**:
- Cytokines and chemokines released by mast cells (e.g., IL-4, IL-5, TNF-α) recruit eosinophils, neutrophils, basophils and Th2 cells, causing renewed swelling, airway narrowing and tissue inflammation
patches.reason: Leukotrienes and PGD2 are newly synthesized within minutes as part of the early reaction; the late phase is driven by recruited leukocytes.

patches.old: Epinephrine is the only appropriate treatment for anaphylaxis.
patches.new: Intramuscular epinephrine is the first-line, essential treatment for anaphylaxis; antihistamines and corticosteroids are only adjuncts.
patches.reason: Epinephrine is first-line, but other supportive treatments (fluids, oxygen, adjunct drugs) are also used.

patches.old: Immune complexes form when antigen and antibody are present in roughly equivalent concentrations.
patches.new: The pathogenic complexes are small, soluble ones that form in slight antigen excess; large complexes formed near equivalence are cleared efficiently by phagocytes, whereas small ones escape clearance and deposit in tissues.
patches.reason: Tissue-depositing immune complexes form in antigen excess, not at equivalence.

patches.old: Induration (not just redness) of ≥10 mm at 48–72 hours indicates prior sensitization (past infection or BCG vaccination).
patches.new: Induration (not just redness) is read at 48–72 hours; it is called positive at ≥5, ≥10 or ≥15 mm depending on the person's risk group, and indicates prior sensitization (past infection, or cross-reactivity from BCG vaccination or nontuberculous mycobacteria).
patches.reason: CDC uses three risk-based cutoffs, not a single 10 mm threshold.

visual.title: The four hypersensitivity types
visual.alt: Four columns. Type I (immediate, IgE): allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells; histamine, leukotrienes and PGD2 within minutes; a late phase hours later with eosinophils and Th2 cells; examples anaphylaxis, hay fever, allergic asthma; clue raised IgE and eosinophils. Type II (antibody against cell or matrix antigens): IgG or IgM causes complement lysis, phagocytosis, ADCC, or blocks or stimulates a receptor; examples transfusion reaction, hemolytic disease of the newborn, Goodpasture, myasthenia gravis, Graves; clue positive Coombs test. Type III (immune complexes): small complexes formed in slight antigen excess deposit in vessels, glomeruli and joints, activating complement and neutrophils; examples serum sickness, Arthus, SLE, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis; clue low C3 and C4. Type IV (delayed, T cells): Th1 cells activate macrophages via IFN-gamma or CD8 T cells kill, peaking at 48 to 72 hours with no antibody; examples PPD test, contact dermatitis, granulomas.
visual.caption: Ask two questions: is antibody involved, and is the antigen on a cell, in a soluble complex, or seen by T cells?
